hook_text: That R40 chicken actually costs R45. Someone else is quietly paying the difference.
clip_script: A chicken farm sits upstream. A village sits downstream. The farm sells chickens at forty rand, thousands of them — the market working, apparently. Now stand in the village. The river arrives carrying the farm's runoff. Water must be boiled — paraffin costs money. Kids get stomach bugs — clinic, taxi, missed school. The riverside gardens yield less. Add it honestly: every chicken costs the village about five rand in coping. But no bill for that five rand ever reaches the farm — or the shopper who thinks a chicken costs forty. It doesn't. It costs forty-five: forty at the till, five in paraffin and lost spinach. Economists call the missing five an external cost, and here's what the lie does: because chickens LOOK cheaper than they are, people buy MORE of them — the market over-produces exactly the thing hurting the village. Not from malice. From a missing bill. The fix? Send it. A five-rand levy per chicken, sized to the real damage. Now the price tells the truth, buyers buy less, and the levy can clean the water. That's every carbon tax and every sin tax you've ever heard of: the hospital bill, delivered in advance, at the till.
visual_style: A split river scene — bright farm upstream, muted village downstream — with tiny red R5 receipts floating downstream unclaimed until a hand stamps one onto the chicken's price tag and the colours rebalance.
mood: Quietly indignant, resolving into satisfaction as the price is corrected.
pacing: Steady accumulation of the village's small costs, one sharp turn at the missing bill, brisk resolution.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and master externalities, the state's toolkit and cost-benefit analysis for Paper 2.
